abstract: |
  A study's protocol, experiment script, analysis pipeline, and publication figures all begin as views of one design, but they drift apart as the study runs, until no single artifact describes the study as it was actually run. What is missing is a shared record of the *process*: cognitive science has mature standards for its data (e.g., BIDS), yet the process that produced the data still lives in scattered text, slides, and custom code. We present *Studyflow*, a visual notation that fills this gap by giving the experimental process a single machine-readable, human-understandable, and executable representation. A study is a typed directed graph, realized as an extension of the Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN 2.0) with the elements experimental research needs: domain-specific activities (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction), decision gateways (randomization, eligibility), data operations, and data elements bound to community standards. One Studyflow file is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis specification, and the publication figure, projected as multiple views for different audiences. We demonstrate the notation end to end with a study in which human participants and a cohort of artificial agents perform the same cognitive tasks from one studyflow diagram, behind one execution interface. One registrable protocol enrolls, runs, and analyzes both populations and reports where they agree and diverge.
impact-statement: |
  A single machine-readable diagram serves as a study's protocol, runnable experiment, analysis specification, and publication figure for both human participants and artificial agents.

# Introduction

## The reproducibility gap is in *processes*, not just data

Every experiment accumulates documents that describe it, and by the end they disagree. A scientific experiment touches many people and systems: a researcher designs it; an ethics committee approves it; a participant runs it; a data pipeline ingests it; a model trains on it; a reviewer reads it as a manuscript; and a replicator tries to rebuild it. Reproducing it later requires more than the data and the manuscript: it requires an explicit, complete description of the *processes* that generated them [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines]. A complete description of any computing system, including experiments, needs both a data model (for its structure and inputs/outputs) and a process model (for its behavior) [@olive2007conceptual].

In cognitive sciences, the processes behind the data are documented mainly in narrative prose, ad hoc lab conventions, box-and-arrow diagrams, or code repositories [@bell2021perspectives; @osc2015; @nosek2022replicability]. The community has strong standards for the data, notably BIDS; the process, a record of how those data came to be, has no equivalent. The asymmetry has measurable consequences: even articles that share open data cannot be easily reproduced, because the process that connects the data to the results stays informal [@cruwell2023badge].

The cost of this missing process model is clearest when someone other than the author reads a study. A battery of tasks, an online study on a recruitment dashboard, or an AI evaluation benchmark each accumulates the same trail: the protocol PDF, the ethics application, the experiment script, the preprocessing notebook, the model card [@mitchell2019modelcards], the manuscript figure, and the participant flow diagram (clinical studies further add registries and acquisition pipelines to this); all begin as views of the same study, and they end as inconsistent ones. An inter-stimulus interval fixed at 500 ms in the protocol ships as 450 ms in the experiment script, is rounded to about half a second in the methods text, and is dropped from the figure caption, so four artifacts disagree about one number and none is authoritative. By that point, no single artifact describes the study *as it was actually run*. Divergence among the artifacts limits how far reviewers and replication studies can independently trust the code and data. Trust in research is built or lost here.

The usual compensation for a missing process model is voluntary narrative reporting (e.g., checklists, preregistration forms, and journal endorsements). The available evidence suggests it has limited effect. A cross-sectional study of 400 psychology articles published in 2022 found that only 7-14% had been preregistered and 14-16% shared raw data (the lower bounds from a broad sample, the upper from prominent journals) [@hardwicke2024prevalence]. Despite more than a decade of data sharing and reproducibility reform, gaps between endorsement and adherence recur across research fields and journal policies [@percie2020arrive; @hair2019iicarus; @hardwicke2024transparency]. The reason is structural rather than a matter of researcher compliance: a checklist records *what to mention* without requiring *what to share*, and it accepts a narrative description of a process in place of a formal, verifiable one. Even preregistration, the strongest of these instruments, fixes a static plan that cannot always track the adaptive designs, data-dependent branches, and mid-study decisions of contemporary studies, and the gap between the registered plan and the executed procedure reopens the moment the study deviates [@claesen2021adherence; @hardwicke2023preregistration]. This is not limited to human research. The sibling field of AI evaluation has reached the same state: a benchmark is an experiment, and no current artifact records its procedure (see Related work). The underlying process model stays implicit, and implicit means open to interpretation.

We argue that reproducibility should be a property of the shared artifact itself, rather than separate documentation kept alongside the work: a single living representation, machine-readable and human-understandable, that keeps the process model and the data model aligned across a study's many audiences. This paper's contribution is one version of that idea, built on a standard process notation.

This paper makes three contributions. First, *Studyflow*, a notation that turns the experimental process into one machine-readable, human-understandable, and executable artifact: a single file that is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis specification, and the publication figure, realized as a domain-specific profile of BPMN 2.0 and projected as four reader-facing views. Second, a formal account of that artifact, a typed attributed graph with explicit well-formedness conditions and view projections, with an open-source modeler and runner that author and execute it. Third, a worked study run end to end from a single file, in which human participants and a cohort of artificial agents perform the same battery of cognitive tasks behind one execution interface.

## Related work

Today each audience of experimental research works with a different artifact, and these artifacts are hard to keep consistent. Existing approaches fall into a few overlapping families, none representing the whole study as one shared, executable artifact; we summarize them here, leaving the per-tool detail to Supplementary Note 2.

**Workflow engines** model analysis as a directed acyclic graph and run it at scale (Galaxy, KNIME, Nextflow, Snakemake, NiPype, the Common Workflow Language) [@thegalaxycommunity2024; @berthold2009; @nextflow; @wirth2024; @cwl; @pydra], but their representations target machines and developers, fit fixed-input data pipelines, and encode study logic in code [@peikert2021reproducible].

**Experiment builders and orchestration platforms** specify and run the behavioral experiment itself: presentation libraries (PsychoPy, jsPsych, lab.js, Gorilla) [@peirce2019psychopy; @deleeuw2015jspsych; @henninger2022labjs; @anwylirvine2020gorilla], online orchestration (oTree, Empirica, PsyNet) [@chen2016otree; @almaatouq2021empirica; @harrison2026psynet], a design layer that compiles stimulus sequences for humans or language models (SweetPea, AutoRA, SweetBean) [@musslick2022sweetpea; @musslick2024autora; @strittmatter2025sweetbean], and machine-readable single-trial state machines (BEADL) [@beadl]. Each specifies one slice, a stimulus sequence, a trial, or a deployment; none spans eligibility, allocation, analysis, and the published figure as one artifact.

**Guidelines and protocol registries** share protocols as free-form text (protocols.io) and catalog reporting guidelines through EQUATOR (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA) [@teytelman2016; @simera2010equator; @hopewell2025consort; @chan2025spirit; @strobe; @page2021prisma], enforcing structure only at reporting time, in prose and PDF; executable publishing makes the analysis narrative runnable but leaves the experimental procedure as text [@maciocci2019era; @lakens2021machinereadable].

**Data standards and ontologies** (BIDS, Psych-DS, CSVW, our Behaverse Data Model, the FAIR principles) [@bids; @psychds; @csvw; @bdm; @fair] make the data machine-readable but say little about the process that produced it.

**Provenance and packaging** (W3C PROV, RO-Crate, Workflow Run RO-Crate, process mining) [@w3cprov; @soilandreyes2022rocrate; @leo2024wfrunrocrate; @vanderaalst2016process] describe what was run retrospectively, not a prospective executable specification, and rarely the experimental context such as eligibility, randomization, or exclusions; Studyflow is complementary, and these standards can package its runs (see Discussion).

**Visual notations** communicate at a glance but are rarely standardized or tied to code [@bogale2024]; BPMN [@bpmnspec], already extended into domain profiles for clinical pathways and machine learning [@braun2014; @tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], and Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009] show the appetite for domain-specific graphical formalization, yet none targets experimental cognitive science.

**AI evaluation harnesses** (HELM, the LM Evaluation Harness, BIG-bench, Inspect) [@liang2023helm; @biderman2024lessons; @srivastava2023bigbench; @aisi2024inspect] and agentic benchmarks [@zhou2024webarena; @xie2024osworld; @mialon2024gaia] standardize scoring, but audits find that what was run is unrecoverable from what was reported [@burnell2023rethink; @reuel2024betterbench], and none extends to a human cohort, eligibility criteria, or publication figures.

**Agents as participants.** A fast-growing literature administers psychology experiments to language models [@binz2023gpt3; @codaforno2024cogbench; @aher2023llms; @argyle2023silicon; @webb2023analogical; @binz2025centaur] under the banner of machine psychology [@rahwan2019machine; @hagendorff2024machinepsych], yet each study re-implements a bespoke prompting harness and matches human and model administration by hand; methodological critiques [@ivanova2025cognitive; @dillion2023replace; @lin2025fallacies] and a consensus reporting checklist [@feuerriegel2026guidellm] now demand exactly what no artifact provides, a pinned, shareable, executable record of how the experiment was administered. The same drive appears in clinical research and the wet lab [@cdisc_odm; @ich2025m11; @beal2022labop], each formalizing one dimension, the regulatory document, the lab procedure, or the analysis plan, none an executable experiment whose subject may, unknowingly, be a person or an artificial agent.

Across these families the same limitations recur: (1) a representation is machine-facing or human-facing but rarely both; (2) experimental details stay informal during planning and execution; (3) records of what happened cover the code that ran but not the experimental decisions around it (who was eligible, how they were allocated, why a trial was excluded); (4) the experiment specifications that do exist cover only one task, one stimulus sequence, or one agent; and no artifact aligns the scientist, engineer, ethics board, funding agency, reviewer, and, increasingly, the AI evaluator. No single representation spans the full study lifecycle in a form that all of them can read, validate, and execute (Figure 1).

## Desiderata for a study specification language

A notation that closes the process gap, and so specifies an experimental study end to end, must satisfy several requirements at once: what the shared artifact *is*, how it behaves, who can read it, and how it stays grounded in existing standards. We state these requirements as seven desiderata. (R1) *A single source of truth*: one artifact serves every audience, so the views cannot drift apart. (R2) *Executable, not merely descriptive*: the specification runs; it does not only document. (R3) *Understandable to every audience without code*: an ethics board, a reviewer, or a collaborator can read it without programming. (R4) *Grounded in standards*: the artifact remains valid in a widely used standard notation and usable by generic tools that do not know the domain-specific extensions. (R5) *Process and data on one artifact*: the procedure and the data it produces are specified together. (R6) *Extensible without forking*: new domains and concepts plug in, not through changes to the core. (R7) *Execution agnostic*: who or what performs the protocol is a runtime decision, not a property of the specification. @tbl-requirements maps each desideratum to where the framework meets it.

## BPMN as a foundation

Meeting these desiderata is a language design problem. Experimental cognitive science meets the standard criteria for a domain-specific language (DSL): recurring structural patterns across studies, expert users who would benefit from a familiar notation rather than general purpose code, and no alternative executable language that already covers the whole experiment lifecycle [@mernik2005dsl]. Rather than invent a new notation, we extend an established one that researchers, engineers, and reviewers already recognize.

Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is a mature graphical language for processes, standardized by ISO [@white2004introduction]. It already provides what scientific workflows need (events, activities, sub-processes, gateways, data objects, sequence and data flows, and choreography), an established tooling ecosystem (`bpmn-js`, Camunda Modeler, and many visualization tools), and a standard serialization, BPMN 2.0 XML, that outlives any single tool. Building on a graphical standard is itself a bet: whether, when, and why visual diagrams beat text is an open empirical question [@moody2009physics; @larkin1987diagram; @figl2017comprehension] that we revisit in Limitations.

We build on two of BPMN's extension mechanisms, `extensionElements` and namespaced attributes, which let authors add elements inside a new namespace [@magnani2009bpdmn]. The same mechanism is used to extend the BPMN core in many other domains [@zarour2019; @braun2014classification]; experimental cognitive science is the gap they leave.

<!--
Recent large language model-assisted BPMN authoring tools (ProMoAI, BPMN-ChatBot, and related work [@kourani2024promoai; @kourani2024process_modeling_llm]) accelerate diagram authoring from text, but evaluations show that competitive syntactic quality does not translate into domain-specific semantics or domain-specific validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Authoring help is welcome; it is not a substitute for a profile that defines what *cognitive task*, *random assignment*, or *eligibility check* mean inside a process model. That profile is the gap Studyflow fills. -->

The rest of the paper is organized around these desiderata: the Studyflow notation is designed to meet them, the worked example exercises them, and the discussion revisits where they hold and where they do not. The framework that follows delivers them as the notation itself and the multiple views it projects for different audiences, demonstrated through an open-source reference implementation that authors and runs Studyflow diagrams (Supplementary Note 1). Together they make tractable a study design that current tooling cannot express in one artifact: a registrable protocol that enrolls human participants and a cohort of artificial agents alike.

# The Studyflow framework

Studyflow represents an entire study as a single diagram: a typed directed graph (realized in BPMN 2.0 format) that holds the protocol, the runnable experiment, the analysis specification, and the publication figure together. The tooling projects a view from that one source for each audience (Views, below). The example in the Results section is one such file: a reviewer reads it as a diagram, the runner app walks it node by node, the analysis code is a handful of typed nodes inside it, and the published CONSORT figure is exported from it. The rest of this section defines that diagram and the views it projects. The reference tooling that authors and runs the diagram is described in Supplementary Note 1, and @tbl-glance summarizes its building blocks.

  - Randomization, stratified allocation, and eligibility, alongside the standard BPMN gateways

  - transform, map, filter, flatMap, reduce, and compose, each able to delegate to an external function (`functionRef`)

## Formal definition

A Studyflow diagram is a typed, attributed directed multigraph $S = (N, E, \mathrm{src}, \mathrm{tgt}, \tau, \lambda)$ over a versioned schema $\Sigma$ (the LinkML schema of Materials and methods). $N$ is a finite set of nodes and $E$ a finite set of edges, with endpoint maps $\mathrm{src}, \mathrm{tgt}: E \to N$. The schema fixes a type alphabet $T$, split into node types $T_N$ (events, activities, gateways, actors, and data elements such as datasets, schemas, and stores) and edge types $T_E$; the typing map $\tau: N \cup E \to T$ assigns each node a type in $T_N$ and each edge a type in $T_E$. The attribution $\lambda$ gives each element a record of typed attributes admissible for its type under $\Sigma$, for example the `instrument` of a cognitive task, the `probabilityFunction` of a random gateway, or the `onset` and `duration` of an activity. Because data elements are themselves nodes of $S$, the data specification and the control flow inhabit one object (R5). @tbl-notation collects the symbols used here and in later sections.

Edge type separates control flow from data flow. The sequence-flow edges $E_{\mathrm{seq}}$ (those $e$ with $\tau(e)$ a sequence flow) induce the control-flow graph $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}} = (N, E_{\mathrm{seq}})$; the data-association edges $E_{\mathrm{assoc}}$ induce the data-flow graph $G_{\mathrm{data}} = (N, E_{\mathrm{assoc}})$. The two share the node set but no edges, so one object holds both the order in which things happen and the data each step reads and writes. Execution is a walk over $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$ (Materials and methods), and the typed pipeline of an analysis is a path in $G_{\mathrm{data}}$ (Results).

A diagram is *well-formed* when five conditions hold: (W1) it derives from the abstract syntax of Supplementary Listing S1; (W2) $\tau$ and $\lambda$ validate against $\Sigma$; (W3) endpoints respect type, so every sequence-flow edge runs between flow nodes (events, activities, gateways) and every data-association edge joins a data element to a flow node; (W4) $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$ is sound, with at least one start event and one end event and every flow node on some path from a start to an end (no dead branches); and (W5) the serialization is valid BPMN 2.0 XML. W1 and W2 are the context-free and schema constraints; W3 and W4 are the static constraints a generic BPMN validator cannot state, and the modeler checks them by simulation before a study runs (Supplementary Note 1).

$G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$ is directed but not acyclic, because experimental procedures contain interrupts, loops, and multi-agent exchanges. Boundary events, message flows, and choreography express these, which a directed acyclic graph represents only through external control logic.

::: {#tbl-notation .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l" tbl-colwidths="[36,64]"}
Notation used in the formal definition and reused throughout.

- - Symbol
  - Meaning

- - $S = (N, E, \mathrm{src}, \mathrm{tgt}, \tau, \lambda)$
  - A Studyflow diagram: nodes, edges, endpoint maps, the typing $\tau$, and the attribution $\lambda$

- - $\Sigma$
  - The versioned schema fixing the type alphabet and admissible attributes

- - $T_N$, $T_E$
  - Node types and edge types

- - $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$, $G_{\mathrm{data}}$
  - The control-flow and data-flow graphs, over the shared node set $N$

- - $\pi_p(S)$
  - A view: the projection of $S$ selected by a predicate $p$

- - W1-W5

- - R1-R7

:::


**A standard notation.** Studyflow realizes this object as a domain-specific profile of BPMN 2.0 [@white2004introduction], tailored to experimental cognitive science. The diagrams stay valid BPMN 2.0 XML and open in any compliant tool, and BPMN's extension mechanism (`extensionElements`, namespaced attributes) adds the domain semantics of $T$ and $\lambda$ without breaking the base standard [@stroppi2011; @magnani2009bpdmn]. Studyflow deliberately leaves BPMN's serialization conventions, XML namespaces, element identifiers, and base shapes untouched. The domain extensions live inside BPMN's native extension slot (Serialization, in Materials and methods).

**What Studyflow inherits.** Studyflow reuses BPMN's full vocabulary for control flow and structure: events (start, end, boundary, timer, error), activities (tasks, sub-processes, call activities), the gateway types, sequence and message flows, data objects and stores with their associations, pools and lanes, and choreography for multi-agent interactions. These elements keep standard BPMN shapes and behave as the OMG specifies [TODO: add OMG ref].

**What Studyflow adds.** Four areas extend BPMN with vocabulary experimental research routinely needs. First, a root **study container** groups every other element and carries metadata for the whole study (e.g., title, version, authors, runtime). Second, domain-specific activity types specialize the generic BPMN task with specific kinds (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest, video games, and a curated cognitive battery); each shows a distinctive icon but remains a normal BPMN task underneath. Third, domain-specific data elements add bindings to community schemas (BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], BDM, [@bdm], CSVW) on top of BPMN's generic data objects. A data operation marker tags an activity with the kind of transformation it performs (transform, map, flatMap, reduce, filter, compose) and, optionally, a `functionRef` reference to an external function (`scheme://ref@version`) with an `arguments` block, so the data flow stays visible while the work itself can delegate to a Python callable, container, or script. Fourth, additional gateways encode branching patterns specific to experimental design. A random gateway for randomization, a stratified allocation gateway, and an eligibility gateway that lists inclusion and exclusion criteria. Optional temporal attributes (onset, duration, progress) attach to activities and events, so the Gantt view derives schedules and trial timing from the same diagram. @tbl-elements gives a representative subset.

These added features split into a small core and optional domain extensions (Figure 2). The core covers the language scaffolding and a companion cognitive layer, while four optional layers cover specific domains (see Materials and methods). New domains plug in by writing a schema, without changing the core or tooling. Supplementary Table S1 has the complete catalog.

**A machine-readable specification.** The core language is defined by a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that the BPMN tooling reads (Materials and methods). Listing 1 gives the schema for the study container and a cognitive task: a `CognitiveTask` specializes a generic data operation activity, requires an `instrument`, and carries an inline `configurations` block. Supplementary Listing S2 shows how a research gateway maps onto BPMN: a `RandomGateway` and an `EligibilityGateway` both specialize a standard `bpmn:ExclusiveGateway`, so they serialize and render as ordinary BPMN gateways while carrying the attributes that make randomization and eligibility explicit.

**Listing 1.** Studyflow language specification (LinkML excerpt; descriptions abridged). The schema fixes element types, required attributes, and validation rules independently of any tool.

```yaml
Study:
  class_uri: bpmn:Process
  tree_root: true
  attributes:
    name:
      range: string
      required: true
    version:
      range: string
    authors:
      range: string
      multivalued: true
    runtime:
      range: RuntimeEnum

CognitiveTask:
  is_a: DataOperationActivity        # a specialized BPMN activity
  class_uri: cognitive:CognitiveTask
  attributes:
    instrument:                      # psychopy, jspsych, labjs, ...
      range: string
      required: true
    configurations:                  # instrument-specific, inline YAML
      range: YAMLString
```


## Views: Study, Gantt, Checklist, and Figure

Each view is a *projection* of the formal study object. Given a predicate $p$ over elements, the view $\pi_p(S)$ is the sub-structure of $S$ induced by $\{x \in N \cup E : p(x)\}$, carrying each kept element's identity and attributes $\lambda(x)$ unchanged and forgetting the rest. The four views are four predicates: the Study view takes $p \equiv \mathrm{true}$; the Gantt view keeps the elements whose $\lambda$ carries an `onset` or `duration` and places them on a time axis; the Checklist view keeps the elements carrying a `checklist` attribute and forgets all structure but that attribute; and the Figure view takes $p(x) = \lambda(x).\mathit{visible}$, rendering the kept elements while its export still embeds all of $S$ as metadata, so a published figure stays runnable (Figure view, below). *Consistency.* A projection only forgets; it never adds or rewrites. Any element kept by two views therefore carries the same identity and attributes in both, since both read them from the one $S$; the views are pairwise consistent by construction, the operational content of the single source of truth (R1). A single `.studyflow` diagram therefore renders in four ways, each suited to a different stakeholder (Figure 3); editing $S$ updates every $\pi_p(S)$ at once, and no view is edited independently.

**Study view.** The default rendering is a BPMN-like graph that shows every element and connection. It is *structural*, showing what happens and in what order, and it serves methodology sections, reviewers checking logical structure, and developers setting up data flow.

**Gantt view.** A Gantt-style rendering places elements that carry timing along a time axis. BPMN has timer events but no native way to express activity duration, scheduled onset, or progress, so Studyflow attaches these as optional attributes on activities and events: *onset*, *duration*, and *progress* (percentage or label). Resource allocation uses BPMN pools and lanes directly to group rows, with no separate attribute. When the temporal attributes are present the same mechanism scales from timing of a trial (stimulus duration, ITI, response window) to the timing of a study (visit schedule, follow-ups). In this view, milestones appear as elements with zero duration. It suits longitudinal studies and schedules of enrolment and assessment as in SPIRIT [@spirit2013].

**Checklist view.** This task-oriented view flattens the diagram into a list of items and status, drawn from an optional `checklist` attribute on every element. It supports two use cases: *running studies day to day* (what is next, what is done) and *adhering to reporting guidelines* (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA, and CARE), where guideline items map to the elements that satisfy them, so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. Checklists ship inside the `.studyflow` file.

**Figure view.** The Figure view renders a diagram as a publication-ready image in which annotations on each element decide what is shown or hidden. A manuscript figure usually needs a curated subset of the full diagram, the protocol without the data layer or a single highlighted path through a branch, so rather than redraw by hand, an author marks elements to show or hide and exports the curated SVG. The exported image (e.g., SVG format) embeds the complete `.studyflow` source as metadata, so a deposited figure is the runnable file itself rather than a picture of the study: a reader can open it in any conformant tool, and re-run it (Journal production pipelines typically re-encode figures and strip embedded metadata, so for published articles the same guarantee is delivered by shipping the `.studyflow` file as the figure's source data). Because the visibility annotations live in the same file as the rest of the diagram, the figure stays valid BPMN and tied to the study it depicts. This is the mechanism behind the published CONSORT-style figure.

A specification is credible only if something runs it. Two reference applications (MIT licensed) serve as reference implementations: a modeler that authors, validates, and exports diagrams, and a runner that walks a participant or an artificial agent through a diagram node by node behind one interface (see Supplementary materials for more details).

# Results

This section follows one study from protocol to publication. Human participants and a cohort of artificial agents perform the same battery of six cognitive tasks, each allocated to a self-paced or a time-pressured path, and we ask where the two groups agree and where they diverge. The agent cohort table (@tbl-agents) describes the families of agents, and the battery table (@tbl-battery) describes the six tasks. The same file is the input at every stage (see Data availability).

## Design

The example study asks an agreement question: across the six tasks, do humans and artificial agents perform alike, and where do they diverge? Both measures are fixed in the protocol before the study runs. Agreement is an equivalence test on accuracy per task; divergence is how well a classifier tells humans from each agent family, scored as AUC against chance level (see analysis stage, below).

Each subject is allocated to a self-paced or a time-pressured path, with task order randomized per subject within the path. Time pressure means different things across families of subjects, an enforced response window for humans, a deadline in the prompt for language models, a pondering budget for the recurrent model. So the contrast between paths is read only within a family.

We give the study the structure of a randomized controlled trial, following the CONSORT guidelines. The protocol carries what a registered study needs, including consent, eligibility screening, and random allocation to the two paths. The protocol file (a SVG image with embedded studyflow) is deposited on OSF [TODO: OSF link].

In current practice corresponding document trail of such study is spread across a registry entry, a PDF for ethics approval, a recruitment system, and a CONSORT flow diagram drawn at write-up, none of them a machine-readable view of the others [@moher2012; @rennie2001; @hopewell2025consort].

We start from the CONSORT 2025 reference diagram. Figure 4 compares different ways of plotting CONSORT: (a) the standard CONSORT 2025 reference flow as published by the CONSORT group, (b) a Studyflow reproduction encoded with the same labels and pathways, and (c) an annotated comparison whose right path uses the traditional text and box treatment (i.e., CONSORT for reporting) and whose left path uses boundary error events (i.e., CONSORT for execution).

The key mechanical difference between the traditional figure and the executable encoding is how attrition is represented. In the traditional figure, each "Excluded / Did not receive / Lost to follow-up / Discontinued" box sits beside the activities as an annotation, and readers must infer that these counts subtract from the main flow. In the executable representation, attrition is encoded as a *boundary error event* attached to the activity that participants left from. Exclusion at screening hangs off the eligibility gateway, non-receipt of intervention leaves the two allocation tasks, loss to follow-up and discontinuation off the follow-up tasks, and exclusion from analysis off the analysis tasks. Each event ends in an error end event. This has three consequences. First, the diagram's topology now matches the trial's topology that is used to run data collection, so a participant lost during follow-up exits along an edge that starts at the follow-up activity itself, rather than a side annotation. Second, the flow arithmetic becomes clear and verifiable by machine: at every activity, inflow equals outflow plus attrition. A runner app can write counts onto activities and attrition counts onto the error end events. Third, the boundary error event is BPMN's standard primitive for interrupts, inheriting its execution semantics for exception handling [@bpmnspec; @dijkman2008semantics].

In the studyflow file, each attrition path is a few lines of standard BPMN: a boundary error event wired to an error end event whose count is a typed attribute:

```xml
<bpmn2:boundaryEvent id="Dropout" attachedToRef="Battery">
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_Dropout_Excluded</bpmn2:outgoing>
  <bpmn2:errorEventDefinition id="ErrorDef_Dropout" />
</bpmn2:boundaryEvent>
<bpmn2:endEvent id="Dropout_End" name="Dropped out (n=...)">
  <bpmn2:extensionElements>
    <studyflow:attrition count="..." />
  </bpmn2:extensionElements>
  <bpmn2:errorEventDefinition errorRef="ErrorDef_Dropout" />
</bpmn2:endEvent>
```

The diagram carries domain semantics alongside the BPMN structure. The enrollment start event references the consent participants see, so an ethics board approves the same consent that a runner app renders when it reaches this node. The screening task carries a checklist that drives the *Checklist* view (the demographics, medical history, and baseline screen items shown are from the CONSORT reference template); the eligibility and randomization gateways carry those types; each cognitive task declares its own parameters (e.g., for the N-back: the N, stimulus duration, inter-trial interval, and trials per block); and the allocation, follow-up, and analysis tasks carry checklists describing protocol obligations. Together, these layers render as the CONSORT diagram while also being runnable and a checklist.

Where CONSORT structures the *report*, SPIRIT structures the *plan*. The same study also renders as a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, its checklist items mapping onto the Gantt view [@chan2025spirit; @spirit2013]. A SPIRIT plan and a CONSORT report are then the same file at two points in its lifecycle: the schedule before randomization, and the flow diagram with attrition counts written into the boundary events once the study has run.

The same flow runs an artificial agent wherever it runs a human participant (next section). CONSORT and SPIRIT were written for human trials, and routing an artificial agent cohort through the same flow is notational rather than a claim about the agents (see Discussion).

## Enroll and run

The runner app now walks the diagram node by node, the same way for a participant or an agent.

**The cognitive battery.** Our study administers a Behaverse battery of six cognitive tasks including tasks conventionally associated with working memory (N-back [@owen2005nback; @redick2013nback] and digit span [@richardson2007span]), attention (multiple-object tracking [@pylyshyn1988mot]), processing speed (pattern comparison [@salthouse1991speed]), fluid reasoning (matrix reasoning [@raven2000matrices]), and set shifting (card sorting [@grant1948sorting]). Task and construct variance are confounded here and humans and agents are therefore compared at the task level throughout. The construct words name lineages, not measurement claims. Each task runs multiple trials per subject. The N-back serves as the worked example below, and the other five use the same machinery.

::: {#tbl-battery .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l,l,l" tbl-colwidths="[26,24,12,38]"}
The subset of selected cognitive tasks from Behaverse battery and the associated construct (not a measurement claim).

- - Task
  - Construct (lineage)
  - Reference

- - N-back
  - Working memory
  - [@owen2005nback; @redick2013nback]

- - Digit span
  - Working memory
  - [@richardson2007span]

- - Multiple-object tracking
  - Attention
  - [@pylyshyn1988mot]

- - Pattern comparison
  - Processing speed
  - [@salthouse1991speed]

- - Matrix reasoning
  - Fluid reasoning

  - Set-shifting
  - [@grant1948sorting]
:::


**Enroll, allocate, and follow up.** We authored the battery as one diagram that orchestrates the four CONSORT stages: enrollment through consent and baseline questionnaires, an eligibility gateway, randomized allocation to the self-paced and time-pressured paths, and follow-up through the six tasks. Each task is itself a set of trial blocks (a warm-up, the test blocks, and any adaptive staircase) that common methodology prose may flatten but the diagram keeps explicit. Once loaded into a study runner app, the diagram is checked for required parameters and then walked one node at a time (Supplementary Figure S3). Randomness policy fixes the subject's path, task order, stimulus order, and every random branch (Materials and methods). Each agent runs [TODO: k] times under recorded sampling parameters and its performance is reported aggregated over runs. The same flow runs for artificial agents and human participants alike.

**Encoding the trials.** Figure 5 places the traditional figure of the N-back task (as slides) next to the studyflow equivalent. The traditional slide is intuitive but underspecified: timing values often live only in the caption, the boundary between trial and block stays implicit, and decisions like "what counts as a correct match" are buried in the analysis code. Studyflow instead encodes the trial as an explicit subgraph: a stimulus activity, a boundary timer for the response window, a second for the inter-trial interval, and annotations and explicit code reference labeling the target and non-target branches. The trial-by-trial encoding in Figure 5 is illustrative; for runs beyond a handful of trials the same logic compresses into a single cognitive task whose parametrization declares the N, trial count, stimulus type, duration, and inter-trial interval, which the runner expands into individual trials (Listing 2). The same parametrization format applies to every task in the battery. Each trial is logged to a standard data format (BDM [@bdm]): the data schema fixes the CSV columns and the diagram fixes their use.

**Listing 2.** The N-back task serialized in a `.studyflow` file (BPMN 2.0 XML, abridged; the stimulus stream is truncated for display). The task is a standard `bpmn:Task` carrying a `behaverse:Task` extension that clarifies the parametrizations such as the N level, the stimulus stream, and the timing.

```xml
<bpmn2:task id="Task_NB" name="N-back (digits)">
  <bpmn2:extensionElements>
    <behaverse:task scene="NB">
      <cognitive:configurations>Blocks:
  NB2:
    Parameters:
      NValue: 2
      Feature: Digits
      Streams:
        - StimulusValue:
            Sequence: {Type: Ordered, Values: [3, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1]}
      StreamSize: 12
      StimulusDisplayDuration: 0.5
      InterStimulusInterval: 1.5
Timelines:
  Main:
    blocks:
      - name: NB2</cognitive:configurations>
    </behaverse:task>
  </bpmn2:extensionElements>
  <bpmn2:incoming>Flow_B_Start_NB</bpmn2:incoming>
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_NB_DS</bpmn2:outgoing>
</bpmn2:task>
```

**One executor, many actors.** The runner administers every actor through one interface. Per trial it sends the stimulus, the allowed response options, the timing constraint, and where needed rendered frames, and records the response and, where applicable, the response time. Each actor keeps its own state locally, a participant's session, an agent's policy, a recurrent hidden state, or a language model's context.

This example study fills the executor with three kinds of actor behind the one interface, plus a uniform random baseline that represents chance level. The *human* actor renders each trial in the GUI participants see and blocks until a person responds (Materials and methods). *Recurrent cognitive models* run through CogPonder [@ansarinia2023cogponder], a differentiable PonderNet-based model that returns both a response and a response time. *Language model agents* run through a proxy package that sends each trial to the configured language model with a trait prompt (below); models with vision input also read the rendered frame [@schulzebuschoff2025visual; @tangtartharakul2026deficits]. Response time is interpretable only where the actor produces it as behavior: measured for humans, predicted by the model for the recurrent family; language models yield elapsed latency, logged as infrastructure metadata and excluded from any latency analysis (@tbl-agents shows the response time interpretation per family).

If an actor replies outside the allowed response options, the runner records the raw reply and flags the trial as missing; no response is imputed. A run whose rate of failed trials exceeds [TODO: threshold]% on any task exits through the boundary error event of the CONSORT and is counted in the participant flow, so agent dropout goes through the same edge as human loss to follow-up. Failed trials are typed by failure mode (refusal, parse failure, timeout), reported in @tbl-agents. The full executor configuration is pinned to every run (Materials and methods) [@ivanova2025cognitive; @lampinen2024content].

**The agent cohort.** We profile a matrix of agents over the whole battery, crossing three factors within each path. *Model*: a uniform random baseline, a recurrent model (CogPonder), several large language models served locally through Ollama, and a commercial vision-language model. *Trait*: response profiles drawn from human characterizations, a careful persona (a conservative decision criterion [@ratcliff2008diffusion]), a fatigued persona (intermittent attentional lapses [@robertson1997oops]), and a fast, error-prone persona (the speed-accuracy trade-off [@wickelgren1977sat]). The manipulation differs by family (a prompt for language models [@argyle2023silicon; @aher2023llms], the pondering cost for the recurrent model), so effects are read within a family. Trait prompts name a disposition, never a target accuracy, so they do not steer the agreement estimate. *Task*: the six battery tasks. Each model also runs a baseline mode with no trait prompt. Agents are allocated exhaustively with [TODO: k] runs per condition as a factorial allocation rather than a randomized allocation, so the CONSORT allocation applies only to the human participants, and studyflow file clarifies that rather than hiding the allocation.

@tbl-agents reports accuracy, the rate of failed trials, and response time where it is a behavioral measure, for every condition, and Figure 6 shows these profiles across tasks against the human reference band [TODO: values from the runs]. Rather than rank many models on a single task, a choice that itself may move rankings [@dehghani2021lottery], we vary the diagram (task, response window, trait) and measure a cohort of agents over a battery of parametrically related items, the design that recent AI evaluation literature has begun to call for [@wang2026psychometrics; @bean2025construct]. The nearest existing artifacts make the differentiation concrete: CogBench scores many language models on seven fixed paradigms behind one harness [@codaforno2024cogbench], and Psych-101 transcribes 160 experiments into text [@binz2025centaur]. Here the same protocol administers both, and the task battery re-parameterizes from the diagram.

## Measure agreement

This stage answers the agreement question and closes the CONSORT flow by counting the analysis exclusions. Such analysis is usually a script whose structure lives in code and comments; here it is a typed pipeline of data operations, so the kind of work each step does is visible in the studyflow diagram.

We analyze the trials through a pipeline of six steps:

- *read* the raw trials;
- *filter* out invalid trials (RT < 100 ms, missing data, flagged rows), the analysis exclusion of the CONSORT flow;
- *map* each trial to its derived measures;
- *branch* at an exclusive gateway on the comparison of interest (i.e., only one branch is selected);
- *reduce* in two steps, first to summaries for each actor (or each run) and then to group-level statistics;
- *render and write*, after a manual review of outliers, the summary table and figures, each to a dataset with a declared schema.

Any of these steps can run inline or delegate to external code: a `functionRef` reference (`python://pkg.fn@1.2`, `docker://image`, or a script URL) names the function and an `arguments` block supplies its parameters, so the diagram shows each step's type, inputs, and outputs while the implementation lives in pinned external code.

The agreement estimand is encoded as typed analysis nodes. For task $t$ and agent family $g$, let $\Delta_t^g = \bar a_t^g - \bar a_t^H$ be the difference in mean accuracy between that family and the humans. The equivalence test declares agreement on task $t$ when the two one-sided tests (TOST) reject at level $\alpha$, that is, when the level-$(1-2\alpha)$ confidence interval for $\Delta_t^g$ falls within the margin $\delta_t$:
$$
\operatorname{agreement}(t,g) \iff \operatorname{CI}_{1-2\alpha}\!\left(\Delta_t^g\right) \subset (-\delta_t,\ \delta_t).
$$
The margin $\delta_t$ and the level $\alpha$ are attributes of the analysis node justified from test-retest variability of the battery. A second, item-level output is the correlation of per-item accuracy between cohorts. The prespecified test is an element of the registered studyflow file, so the registered and executed analyses are essentially the same. The diagram makes three things explicit that code leaves implicit: the conditional branch is a decision gateway in the topology, not an `if` like others; the manual outlier review is a visible node (as a human-in-the-loop manual task); and the output table carries its schema.

Activities sit on the sequence-flow graph $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$, while data and schemas sit on the data-flow graph $G_{\mathrm{data}}$ that BPMN data associations connect (drawn as dashed edges per BPMN 2.0 standard). Every dataset declares its format (BDM, BIDS, Psych-DS) and a schema; tabular data carries a CSVW body or a schema reference [@hoytO3GuidelinesOpen2024; @csvw], while non-tabular data documents tensor dimensions, dtypes, and units. Bindings to BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], and BDM [@bdm] are typed contracts, so an analyst can confirm from the diagram alone that a downstream task consumes exactly the column an upstream task produced.

Concretely, Figure 7 shows the RT analysis subprocess beside the code it runs. The diagram names that code through a `functionRef` reference and encodes the same chained pipeline a programmer would write as `filter |> mutate |> group_by |> summarize`, but it adds two commitments. First, the inputs and outputs are typed (BDM-formatted trials in, models out) and physically stored in a data store (a Parquet file in our example). Second, the analysis task's operation marker declares which primitive operations the task may perform, so tooling can reject any implementation that touches missing columns or runs an unauthorized operation.

Preregistration of analysis then becomes the diagram itself. In current practice a preregistered plan is free text on a registry website, with no link to the specific part of the code that eventually runs. Preregistered studies routinely deviate without disclosure [@claesen2021adherence; @hardwicke2023preregistration], a prominent replicability demonstration was retracted after its analyses were found not to match its own registration [@bakcoleman2024rigour], and tooling now uses language models to compare the registration against the paper post hoc [@cummins2026regcheck]. Machine-readable hypothesis tests made the statistics checkable [@lakens2021machinereadable], and structured preregistration made the plan itself machine-readable [@peters2023preregr]. Under the studyflow encoding the same logic extends to the whole process: the diagram is the spec, the pipeline is one valid implementation linked in the spec, and any divergence between the two shows up as a diff rather than a manual prose comparison.

## Model agreement

The analysis stage reads agreement off group summaries. For task $t$ and agent family $g$, a classifier $f_{t,g}$ predicts the population label from per trial features (responses and accuracy), and its discriminability is the area under the ROC curve, estimated under cross-validation grouped by subject. Two actors are indistinguishable on task $t$ when this score does not exceed the empirical chance level $c_{t,g}$ obtained by permuting the labels:
$$
A_{t,g} = \operatorname{AUC}(f_{t,g}), \qquad \text{indistinguishable on } t \iff A_{t,g} \le c_{t,g}\ \ (c_{t,g} \approx \tfrac{1}{2}),
$$
and they separate where $A_{t,g}$ exceeds $c_{t,g}$. The same machinery extends to a model of the response time distribution for the actor families whose latencies are interpretable, or, with neural recordings, a multimodal predictor. The classifier is authored in the same diagram as the rest of the analysis. ML pipelines fragment the same way experimental protocols do [@kapoor2023leakage], with the model card [@mitchell2019modelcards], feature engineering, training script, deployment, and retraining scattered across repositories. Studyflow's data operations, gateways, and data elements bound to schemas apply to them as cleanly as to behavioral analyses, so an analysis and a training pipeline share one notation with different elements [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml].

## Report

The lifecycle closes where it began, with the reporting guidelines that shaped the design. The *Figure* view exports the CONSORT diagram from the protocol itself, with the attrition already written into the boundary events, so nothing is redrawn at write-up time (Figure 8). The same strategy can provide the specification of the agreement benchmark. See Listing 3 for the full deviation report between the registered `.studyflow` file and the same file after the run.

**Listing 3.** The deviation report of the example study: the diff between the `.studyflow` file deposited at registration and the same file after the run. The protocol's topology and parameters are untouched.

```diff
--- registered.studyflow
+++ as_run.studyflow
-  <bpmn2:endEvent id="Dropout_End" name="Dropped out (n=...)">
+  <bpmn2:endEvent id="Dropout_End" name="Dropped out (n=[TODO])">
     <bpmn2:extensionElements>
-      <studyflow:attrition count="" />
+      <studyflow:attrition count="[TODO]" />
```

Reporting against a guideline then becomes a property the diagram can be checked for, rather than a PDF manually assembled alongside it. Each guideline is, in structure, a controlled vocabulary, a checklist, and sometimes a flow diagram, and Studyflow handles all of them the same way: checklist items become entries in the attributes, flow diagrams become the studyflow file renderings, and vocabulary becomes labels on activities, gateways, and data elements. Items without structural counterparts (harms, blinding, sample-size rationale) map to documentation on elements or references to external resources.

[TODO: rewrite for coherency; hard to read] The pattern recurs across other guidelines. PRISMA 2020 [@page2021prisma] standardized the study flow diagrams that are visual instances of what Studyflow generalizes, TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier] makes intervention details explicit items that map onto the participant branch, and ARRIVE 2.0 [@percie2020arrive], with its history of endorsement without adherence, supplies the animal-research counterpart. The newest entry is telling: a consensus reporting checklist for language model studies in behavioral science now exists [@feuerriegel2026guidellm], and the worked study already records its core items in machine-readable form (Materials and methods). The benchmark literature is converging on the same form from the other side: checklists for benchmark quality [@reuel2024betterbench; @zhu2025abc] are, in structure, EQUATOR-style reporting guidelines, and they map onto the Checklist view exactly as CONSORT items do.

Reporting guidelines and execution specifications need not be different artifacts. At publication, the manuscript ships the exported figure, the Checklist view audit against the target guideline, the `.studyflow` file, and the data. From these a reader can see what every element and variable means, and where, in our case, humans and agents agree or diverge across a set of cognitive tasks.

# Discussion

## What Studyflow changes: from divergent artifacts to one auditable diagram

Current practice keeps the *protocol*, the *code*, and the *figure* as three separate artifacts that begin in agreement and drift apart over a project's life. Studyflow consolidates them into one file, the single source of truth: the same CONSORT diagram is the participant flow figure, the spec a reviewer audits, and the artifact the data collection application steps through, so they can no longer drift apart. The inter-stimulus interval of the Introduction, four values across four artifacts, becomes one attribute in one file, and every view inherits it. That source is plain XML, so it diffs in Git and embeds in image metadata, bringing procedural specifications under the version control discipline that already governs data and code.

Because one protocol serves many actors, a human and agent agreement study becomes one auditable artifact. The same source runs human participants and artificial agents behind one execution interface, and the worked example uses this to author a study in which humans and a cohort of artificial agents are co-subjects, in the notational sense defined above. This supplies the standardized, auditable, multi-executor evaluation protocol that agreement-based analyses presuppose on the measurement side [@nayebi2026alignment]: a fixed task space (here six cognitive tasks, not safety values) and one executable protocol for every actor. For AI evaluation the artifact sits in a recognizable lineage: model cards and datasheets document models and data [@mitchell2019modelcards; @gebru2021datasheets], and evaluation cards have been proposed for evaluations themselves [@dhar2025evalcards]. In those terms, a `.studyflow` benchmark is an eval card a third party can execute. A benchmark no longer needs to be written three times in three formats, and, unlike existing agentic benchmarks whose human baselines are collected outside the benchmark artifact [@mialon2024gaia], here the human and agent cohorts are enrolled, allocated, excluded, and analyzed through the same file.

One property underlies them all, promised in the Introduction and exercised by the worked study: reproducibility becomes a feature of the shared artifact, not of documentation kept beside it.

## Relationship to existing ecosystems

Studyflow sits at the intersection of several ecosystems, and it does not aim to replace any of them.

**Workflow engines and evaluation harnesses.** A family of engines solves a problem Studyflow leaves alone: scalable, reproducible execution on heterogeneous compute, among them Nextflow, the Common Workflow Language (CWL), the Workflow Description Language (WDL), Pegasus, Apache Airflow, Kedro, NiPype, and Pydra [@zhao2008scientific_workflows; @cuevasvicenttin2013workflows; @nextflow; @cwl; @pydra]. The two are complementary. Where a DAG fits data pipelines with fixed inputs and outputs, Studyflow sits *above* such systems: a task can reference an external script (a Nextflow process, a Kedro node, a NiPype workflow), and a downstream tool can compile the protocol diagram into an executable graph [e.g., @ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health]. The same complementarity holds for AI evaluation harnesses [@aisi2024inspect; @biderman2024lessons]: an Inspect task or an lm-eval run is one valid executor behind the runner interface (R7), and the Studyflow file is the protocol it implements. By the same logic, Studyflow leaves process mining to other tools, which can consume its traces directly [@vanderaalst2016process].

**Experiment builders and task specification languages.** SweetBean compiles one stimulus specification to a human or a language model experiment [@strittmatter2025sweetbean], Deliberate Lab runs language model agents as first-class participants alongside humans in real-time group experiments [@tessler2025deliberatelab], and BEADL specifies the state machine inside a single task trial in validated XML [@beadl]; these are the closest existing artifacts to parts of Studyflow, and several are more expressive on their own slice (constraint-solved factorial sampling in SweetPea [@musslick2022sweetpea], adaptive closed-loop designs in AutoRA and PsyNet [@musslick2024autora; @harrison2026psynet], real-time multiplayer in Empirica [@almaatouq2021empirica]). The differentiation is scope and lifecycle: each specifies a stimulus sequence, the state machine of a trial, or a runtime platform, in code or a bespoke format; Studyflow extends an ISO-standard general notation, spans eligibility, allocation, analysis, and reporting, binds to data and reporting standards for the human sciences, and abstracts over three actor families rather than language models alone. A Studyflow cognitive task can carry a SweetPea-generated sequence; the layers compose. Adoption likewise does not ask a lab to rewrite the task it already has: a jsPsych or PsychoPy task referenced by URL becomes the `instrument` of a cognitive task, and the diagram supplies what currently lives around that task in separate documents, the consent, the eligibility rule, the allocation, the data contract, and the figure. For human participants this path runs today (see Limitations).

**Data standards.** BIDS, BDM, Psych-DS, and CSVW prescribe how datasets are structured [@bids; @bdm; @psychds; @csvw]; Studyflow describes the process that produced them and references these standards through dataset, table, and schema elements: a BIDS-typed dataset linked to a "Record EEG" task tells both *what* was collected and *how*.

**Provenance and packaging.** RO-Crate packages research artifacts with metadata for FAIR exchange, and Workflow Run RO-Crate records computational workflow executions [@soilandreyes2022rocrate; @leo2024wfrunrocrate]. These describe retrospectively; Studyflow specifies prospectively and executably, and what its runs record is *behavioral*: the actor, observation, decision, response, and outcome of human and artificial subjects alike, not only the computational graph. The natural interface is packaging a study's `.studyflow` file, exported figure, and trials table as an RO-Crate for deposit, which is how this article's worked example is archived.

**Reporting guidelines.** CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, and STARD enforce structure at the publication stage [@moher2012; @spirit2013; @strobe; @stard]; authored as Studyflow, a guideline carries its checklist items as elements and conformance becomes checkable (Report, in Results).

**Other BPMN profiles.** BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless ML [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], and the human and agent extension [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent] are sibling profiles in adjacent domains, and Studyflow's architecture follows the same pattern. Visual modeling languages established in adjacent fields, such as Systems Biology Graphical Notation in systems biology [@novere2009], confirm both the appetite for graphical formalization and the importance of domain-specific vocabulary [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]. Studyflow also does not aim to be an ontology of experimental design. Process ontologies are numerous but tend to have high upfront cost and low reuse [@norouzi2025semantic_processes], so we have kept the profile small and enforced it by tooling rather than by manual inspection.

A shared architectural pattern across several adjacent systems makes Studyflow's position concrete. LinkML [@moxon2025linkml], NIDM Results [@maumet2016nidm], BIDS [@bids], ISA-Tab [@sansone2012isa], RO-Crate [@soilandreyes2022rocrate], and ARTEM-IS [@styles2021artemis; @soskic2025artemis] share one architecture but occupy *different planes*: a schema layer, a human-friendly authoring layer, and machine-readable outputs, applied respectively to the data model, analysis outputs, data organization, experiment metadata, packaging, and methods reporting. The procedural plane of this architecture, a machine-readable, human-authorable specification of the study *process*, is the gap that Studyflow fills. ARTEM-IS is the closest existing precedent in spirit: it commits the EEG methods reporting community to structured templates that emit both human-readable forms and JSON. Studyflow generalizes the same commitment, from EEG methods reporting to whole procedural specification.

## Objections and alternate views

A profile that spans protocol, execution, analysis, and publication invites objections from both audiences, and we take the strongest in turn. Each is stated as a skeptic would, and each answer concedes what is true before saying what stands.

**"BPMN is heavyweight, and this is one more notation to learn."** This is a fair cost, and we do not claim it away. A reader new to flowcharts still faces a learning curve, gentler than a custom language would impose, because BPMN's visual grammar is already recognized across engineering and analysis [@white2004introduction; @moody2009physics]. We also keep the surface small, a mitigation backed by evidence since comprehension of process models degrades with size and connector count [@reijers2011understandability]. Only two layers always load, the language core and a companion cognitive layer, and everything else is an optional domain layer a study never has to open (Table S1). The bet is that one worked example and a glossary are enough to start.

**"This is just a flowchart with extra labels."** A box-and-arrow figure communicates at a glance, and Studyflow keeps that affordance. The difference is that the same artifact is executable rather than only descriptive (R2): a runner walks the file a reviewer reads, stable identifiers let it diff in Git and embed in an SVG export (R1), and the elements validate against a versioned LinkML schema, so *cognitive task*, *random gateway*, and *eligibility check* carry checkable meaning rather than informal labels [@moxon2025linkml]. A flowchart that an ethics board reads, a participant runs, and a figure exports from one source is doing more than a flowchart.

**"Reading artificial agents as co-subjects in a CONSORT-style study overclaims; CONSORT is for human trials."** We agree that CONSORT was written for human randomized trials, and we do not assert that an agent cohort inherits the ethical or inferential standing of a human cohort. The skeptic's case is well documented: language models are not substitute humans, treating their data as human evidence carries interpretive fallacies, and AI surrogates risk illusions of understanding [@dillion2023replace; @lin2025fallacies; @messeri2024illusions]. Clinical research has so far engaged AI from the inverse direction, as the intervention applied to patients rather than as a subject [@liu2020consortai; @cruzrivera2020spiritai]. The claim stays at the level of notation, in agreement with those critiques rather than against them: the protocol topology is one shape, and because the executor is a runtime decision (R7), the same shape can run either cohort. For agents the scores are operational task performance; whether the tasks measure the same constructs in agents as in humans is itself an open question the shared protocol makes testable [@bean2025construct]. An auditable record of exactly what was administered is a precondition for taking the critiques seriously, not a verdict on agent standing, which remains a question for the ethics and evaluation literatures.

**"A single source of truth is brittle and risks tool lock-in."** A single source does concentrate risk, and the design answers that directly. The core specification is a LinkML schema maintained separately from the modeler (R6), and the artifact on disk is plain BPMN 2.0 XML that opens in any compliant tool and degrades gracefully when a tool does not know the domain extensions (R4) [@white2004introduction; @magnani2009bpdmn]. The modeler is one open-source client of that schema, so a project that abandons our tooling keeps a valid file that no single tool owns. We treat the concentration as the feature and the independence from any single tool as the safeguard.

## Limitations

The scope limits of the current system fall into two kinds, and we keep them apart because conflating them would misstate what the language can express. The first kind is a choice of scope in the *tooling*, where the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time and each gap corresponds to a roadmap item. The reference runner ships a fixed set of step kinds, does not support parallel gateways, falls back to a uniform pick where balanced or blocked allocation is called for (so small samples can realize unbalanced arms), has no counterbalancing primitive beyond seeded order randomization, and does not yet traverse choreography tasks. The multi-actor setup likewise works today for the Behaverse battery, the 22 tasks recognized by our data server, CogPonder, and the runner; a custom PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy] or jsPsych [@deleeuw2015jspsych] task referenced from a diagram still runs for human participants, but the recurrent model and language model adapters would each need a matching bridge to read its stimulus stream and inject responses. Generalizing the trial-level interface beyond this battery is likewise a roadmap item. None of these gaps is a limit of the notation.

The second kind is a deliberate boundary of *what Studyflow is for* rather than a missing feature. Studyflow is a specification of the study process, not a stimulus presentation library, so rendering letters at a fixed retinal angle still requires the assessment battery itself or an external framework reached by URL. The diagram describes which stimulus to show, in what order, under what timing constraint, and what to record; the pixel-level mechanics, including the millisecond timing precision that browser collection bounds [@bridges2020timing; @anwylirvine2021timing], are left to the presentation software and characterized there. The latency readouts in this study are medians over many trials, coarse enough that browser jitter is immaterial. Some designs are also intrinsically awkward to express as directed graphs, including adaptive trials, certain Bayesian sequential designs, and ABAB single-subject designs that need feedback, dynamic re-allocation, or open-ended replay. The choreography and message-flow elements cover some of this, and the rest is current research. A notation also does not solve the measurement problems AI evaluation has named: train-test contamination [@xu2024contamination], prompt sensitivity [@biderman2024lessons], and construct validity [@bean2025construct] survive an auditable protocol; what the protocol adds is a record of exactly what was administered, which any such audit presupposes. For the commercial language model, reproducibility is bounded by provider availability: the run pins the provider's snapshot identifier, while the open-weight arm replicates fully offline.

Two claims central to the paper remain unvalidated, and we mark them as such. We have not measured the legibility of large process and data diagrams against the protocol PDFs, manuscript flow figures, and analysis scripts they replace; classic comparisons of flowcharts against text found advantages in some studies and none in others [@scanlan1989flowcharts; @shneiderman1977flowcharts], so the single source comprehension benefit (R3) is a design goal awaiting a usability study, for which the process model comprehension literature supplies validated measures and designs [@figl2017comprehension]. Adoption is also limited: the tooling ships under the MIT license and runs in the browser, but external uptake is a goal, not a result. Naming these edges is part of the contribution.

## Future directions

The nearest-term direction is community extension. Sibling BPMN extensions in clinical pathways and other domains emerged because a small number of groups committed to the same notation, and Studyflow's layered design is deliberately set up to make new domain extensions cheap, each one being a single schema file plus optional rendering code. The adoption signals we watch for are concrete: domain schemas authored outside our group, studies modeled by labs we have not met, and reporting guideline templates contributed upstream.

Two lines of empirical work would strengthen the evidence base. The first is a usability study with cognitive scientists, comparing Studyflow diagrams against the artifacts they replace to test whether the design measurably reduces effort and error. The second is a set of demonstrations beyond the single study here: a multi-session longitudinal study, a test-retest design, an MLOps pipeline with an audit and training loop, and a larger human and agent benchmark. On the AI side, the natural next step is a bridge that compiles the agent branch of a `.studyflow` protocol into an Inspect or lm-eval task [@aisi2024inspect; @biderman2024lessons], so the same registrable protocol that enrolls a human cohort also ships as a standard eval the existing harness ecosystem can run; a battery specified in Studyflow is likewise directly consumable by foundation models of cognition trained on standardized protocol corpora [@binz2025centaur]. On the same path, the pinned executor configuration (Materials and methods) is a model card in all but type [@mitchell2019modelcards]; promoting those records to typed slots on the Actor element would make the agent's record a contract the validator checks, as dataset bindings already are. The case for the machine-readable protocol itself only grows as discovery moves toward multi-agent laboratories and language models act as both experimenter and subject [@ghareeb2025; @manning2024automated], and alignment research makes the same case from the measurement side [@nayebi2026alignment].

More broadly, experimental science increasingly runs on large datasets and automated pipelines, yet the process that produces a result still has no counterpart to what BIDS gave the data. Studyflow is one candidate for that role: a study read, run, and trusted from a single source rather than a trail of documents about it. A study built this way ends with its documents in agreement, because it has only one.
